processes.description: Risk or accounting asks for the detail behind a month's liquidation values, such as the December liquidation values. Darron Giron forwards the request on to whoever holds the deals and asks when the support can be ready. Once the deal list and volumes are pulled, he sends back a file with the volumes for the liquidations, and it goes to the requester and the shared directory.
steps: Risk or accounting asks for the support behind a month's liquidation values.
The request is forwarded to whoever can pull the deal list and volumes, asking when it will be available.
The deals and volumes behind the liquidated positions are pulled into a file.
The volume file is sent back to the requester and saved to the shared directory.

stalls.summary: The person asking for the support has to ask when it will be available, so the round waits on whoever produces the deal and volume file.

automation.approach: A saved query or report that lists the deals and volumes liquidated in a month and writes a standard support file to the shared directory when the month's liquidation values are posted, so people only check the exceptions instead of rebuilding the file on request.
automation.rationale: Every request asks for the same thing, the deal list and volumes behind the liquidation values, so a fixed file layout fed by one query removes the forward and the wait for the file to be produced.

processes.description: Rounds start either on a schedule, when published price tables such as Western pre-scheduled firm electricity prices are passed on, or on request, when a plant fuel manager asks for historical data or a customer asks for a month's El Paso Topock point price. Staff look up the published index, waiting when Gas Daily is not yet loaded, build comparison spreadsheets such as hot days across two Mays, summarise analyst calls, and assign someone to build a Texas section of the gas fundamentals webpage.
steps: A scheduled report comes due or a trader, originator or customer asks for a price or data set.
Staff look up the published prices or index values in the source data.
If the source is not loaded yet, they wait and check back.
They compile the figures into a table or spreadsheet, or write up an analyst call.
They send or forward the result to the traders, originators or customer who asked.

stalls.summary: A request for index data waits because Gas Daily has not been loaded yet, and the person handling it has to keep checking back.

automation.approach: Load the published price indexes into one stored price table and generate the recurring price reports from it on schedule. Point price requests can then be answered from the table, and the report notes when a source such as Gas Daily has not been loaded yet.
automation.rationale: Much of the work is looking up the same published prices and passing on the same tables. A standard report layout fed from a stored price table cuts the lookups and the checking back, while analysis such as call summaries and fundamentals work stays with people.

work_estimate.rationale: The lightest rounds are a lookup, such as finding a month's published point price or passing on a published price table, around 5 minutes. Heavier rounds mean building a comparison spreadsheet, pulling historical plant data or writing up an analyst call, up to 60 minutes. The mid of 20 minutes reflects the mix. Lookups and recurring tables could come from a price feed; choosing data and summarising analysis stay manual.

processes.description: Rounds start with an ISO market notice (operating procedure updates, market redesign documents, new XML schema releases, a scheduled market simulation), a FERC order or proposed rulemaking, or a CPUC decision. Bill Williams forwards most of them with his reading of what they mean for scheduling: ancillary service charges, underscheduling penalties, price caps, refunds and outage notification. He asks colleagues to meet on an order and sends questions to the ISO. Regulatory staff circulate draft comments for same-day review, and pipeline staff track FERC orders on their own reporting.
steps: An ISO notice, FERC order, proposed rulemaking or CPUC decision arrives, often as an automated ISO notice or forwarded summary.
The desk lead reads it and forwards it with a note on how it affects trading or scheduling.
Colleagues discuss the pros and cons, sometimes in a same-day meeting.
Implementation questions go to the ISO and draft comments are reviewed by the stated deadline.
System changes such as new XML schemas, security upgrades or market simulations are prepared and tested.
Scheduling and settlement practice is adjusted, such as outage notification or charge calculations.

stalls.summary: The PDF versions of the ISO's automation specifications have problems ahead of the market simulation, so they have to be reissued or worked around.
New ISO mechanisms come with open questions the desk has to put to the ISO before go-live, such as target pricing, ADS phase II and a test server for the SI security upgrade.
Draft comments go out with a same-day deadline for review, which leaves little room to work out the effect.

contradictions.summary: A FERC order on refunds is reported as departing from the commission's earlier holdings in the same proceeding without explaining why, following an earlier judge's recommendation on retroactive refunds.
The desk's review of the ISO's real-time market proposal finds that its first two stated goals work against each other.

automation.approach: A tracker that collects ISO notices and FERC and CPUC orders as they arrive and records the effective date, any comment deadline and the systems or charges they touch. It flags the ones that need action, such as schema releases, simulations and test servers, and gives each a standard impact summary form for the desk lead to complete.
automation.rationale: Many rounds start from automated ISO notices that only need sorting, while the real work is judging the effect on scheduling and charges. A standard impact form keeps those judgements, deadlines and open questions to the ISO in one place instead of spread across forwards.

work_estimate.rationale: Automated ISO notices need only a check of whether they touch scheduling, charges or systems, around 10 minutes. A typical round means reading an order or proposal and working out its effect on schedules, ancillary service charges, caps or refunds, around 30 minutes. Reviewing draft comments or preparing for a new XML schema or market simulation runs up to 120 minutes. A tracker could sort notices and pull out the dates; the judgement on impact stays manual.
